1vcnzc.text: Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached systems belonging to a company it previously acquired and stole data. Ransomware group WhiteArmor claimed the attack over the weekend, threatening that it would release about 100GB of information allegedly exfiltrated from the company's logistics and supply-chain platform. Legacy system compromise The investigation into the incident is ongoing, but the shipping firm says that current evidence indicates that "no sensitive data has been disclosed." Maersk added that it does not expect disruptions to operations, and assures customers that they can continue booking and managing shipments through its systems as usual. “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” Maersk states. A.P. Moller–Maersk is a Danish shipping and logistics group and one of the world’s largest container carriers by fleet capacity. The company operates ocean freighters, port terminals, warehouses, and air and land transport services across 130 countries. It has 700 container ships, roughly 13.5% of the global fleet capacity, 60 terminals in 35 countries, and employs 100,000 people. Last year, Maersk reported $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit. Maersk said the incident has been isolated, but did not share details about the affected system, the compromised data types, or when the intrusion occurred. BleepingComputer reached out to Maersk with additional questions, but we have not heard back as of publishing. Ransomware gang claims 100GB data theft Over the weekend, the WhiteArmor ransomware gang listed Maersk on its data leak site and publicly asked for a ransom payment of $5million. "Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world's largest consumer brands. Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA," the threat actor said. "You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin," reads WhiteArmor's public message. WhiteArmor claims to hold approximately 100 GB of data allegedly stolen from Maersk's OCF/LF Logistics platform, which the group is using to support its extortion demands. In 2022, Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the original developer of the OCF/LF Logistics platform, from the Li & Fung Group. According to the threat actor, the data they hold includes nearly 30,000 drivers records, plaintext passwords, 33 SUPER_ADMIN accounts (the most privileged on a system), signed delivery receipts, and 14.44 inventory rows with purchase orders and Advance Shipping Notice (ASNs). The hacker also claims to hold 27,842 mobile device logs that include phone numbers, emails, and IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) numbers. WhiteArmor ransomware lists Maersk, asks for $5 million source: BleepingComputer Maersk noted in the disclosure today that "the incident is isolated to a local system" and that it would notify customers "as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings." "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact," the company advises. In 2017, Maersk was hit by NotPetya ransomware, forcing it to rebuild an infrastructure of over 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. At the time, the company was forced to operate without IT for ten days, incurring damages of up to $300 million. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1sej7d.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments. "In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations. AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times. On its README page, the project maintainer states - Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client. According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions - Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups Read application settings and database connection strings Enumerate debug and error-log directories Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory "On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said. "The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application." The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means. AntiFox Demo Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock. While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company. In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls. "Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said. The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention. The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes. Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus. "The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said. "This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus." According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature. In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases. "In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities." The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution. In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles. Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications. The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort. "Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing." "The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested." Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories - Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares "Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said. "Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

fl088x.text: Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments. The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting. Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities. Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs. “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says. One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory. The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note. Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets. In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects. Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials. The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files. The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks. CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings. Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions. gezkpi.text: For years, eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) has been one of the most celebrated technologies in the Linux kernel. It lets developers run sandboxed programs inside the kernel without writing kernel modules, while powering everything from network monitoring to security tooling. Linux is extremely popular in production servers and giants like Google, Cloudflare, and Meta rely on it daily. The same eBPF capabilities that are attractive for defenders, however, can be a powerful weapon in the hands of attackers. Flare’s research found underground forum posts sharing eBPF rootkit code and step-by-step tutorials. One Russian-language post described how to build an implant with process hiding and packet-triggered activation, and included screenshots the author presented as demonstrations. What Makes eBPF Dangerous? Traditional Linux rootkits typically rely on loadable kernel modules (LKMs) to hook system calls and hide malicious activity. These are well-understood by defenders, and most EDR solutions watch for suspicious module loads. eBPF, however, behaves in a different way. An eBPF malware can hook into kernel functions, observe system calls, or inspect and modify network traffic using the same kernel-supported bpf() interface as legitimate tools like Cilium. Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does. The Next Linux Rootkit Is Already Being Discussed Underground eBPF rootkits are moving from conference talks to underground forum tutorials, and by the time one loads on a host, it’s built to evade your usual checks. Flare monitors forums, marketplaces, and paste sites in real time, so your team sees new tooling, exploits, and chatter early enough to track eBPF threats. Free 2-Week Trial From Classic BPF Backdoors to eBPF Rootkits The first major wake-up call came in 2022 when PwC and Elastic Security Labs documented BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor attributed to a Chinese threat actor tracked as Red Menshen. The BPFDoor sample Elastic analyzed used a classic BPF socket filter to recognize specially crafted TCP, UDP, or ICMP packets. Once triggered, it could open a reverse shell or redirect traffic to the implant. PwC discovered the malware in 2021, and public reporting in 2022 described activity targeting organizations in the Middle East and Asia. Around the same time, Intezer and BlackBerry jointly disclosed Symbiote, a different flavor of Linux malware that weaponizes BPF for stealth. Rather than running as a standalone process, Symbiote uses the dynamic linker to preload a malicious shared library into affected processes. The library intercepts calls to setsockopt() that attach classic BPF filters via SO_ATTACH_FILTER and prepends its own filter instructions to conceal selected traffic from packet capture. Public research had already demonstrated offensive uses of eBPF. In 2021, researchers presented ebpfkit at Black Hat USA and DEF CON. TripleCross combines syscall hooks with XDP and traffic control programs to support library injection, execution hijacking, concealment, and command and control. Boopkit uses getdents64 hooks to hide directory entries. An already installed implant can be triggered remotely in two documented ways, one involving a malformed TCP SYN and the other using ordinary TCP connections. Lastly, in October 2025, Synacktiv reported LinkPro after investigating a compromise that began with an exposed Jenkins server. LinkPro used eBPF programs to hide activity on the host and activate the backdoor when it received a specially crafted packet. Underground Adoption: From Research to Weaponization Security researchers and state-sponsored threat actors have explored how eBPF can be used to build rootkits. Flare’s recent research found underground forum posts sharing code and step-by-step tutorials, showing that these techniques now circulate beyond academic papers and security conferences. On the Russian-language Duty Free forum, a user published a tutorial on building an eBPF rootkit and cited BPFDoor and Symbiote as influences. Screenshot from Flare's platform showing the title and outline of an eBPF rootkit tutorial posted on the Duty Free forum. Sign up for the free trial to access if you aren’t already a customer. The guide includes source code and screenshots that the author presents as demonstrations. It describes how to activate the implant with a TCP SYN packet with a specific window size, hide processes by hooking getdents64, and encrypt command-and-control traffic with AES-256-GCM. The guide also describes using XDP to inspect incoming plaintext HTTP traffic and drop packets that match a list of 43 IP addresses the author associates with antivirus vendors. Flare also identified 10 related Pastebin posts containing XDP packet-processing code and timing thresholds expressed in microseconds. eBPF Beyond Rootkits Flare also found exploit code circulating across multiple platforms. The most frequently reposted exploit (at least six platforms) in the dataset targeted CVE-2017-16995, a 2017 Linux BPF verifier flaw involving incorrect sign extension. Alongside the older eBPF exploits, researchers discovered some fresh exploits. One example is an unverified Linux local privilege escalation PoC targeting kTLS and eBPF sockmaps. The proof-of-concept attempts to corrupt the page cache for /etc/passwd and inject an account with UID 0. Its claim of compatibility with all kernels from 4.18 onward is incorrect. Upstream Linux 4.18 lacks a BPF helper the code calls. Successful privilege escalation on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 has not been verified. In one exploit sample we reviewed, the author credited Claude in a source code comment with generating the BPF instructions. Why Detection Is So Hard The fundamental challenge is that eBPF-based threats operate through a legitimate kernel interface. Unlike a rogue kernel module, an eBPF program passes through the kernel’s built-in verifier and a malicious program that passes verification looks, to the kernel, like any other approved program. Detection today focuses on monitoring bpf() syscalls, tracking loaded programs via bpftool, and watching for suspicious attachment points on sensitive syscalls like getdents64 and execve. But these are reactive measures, and attackers have the advantage of operating through the kernel’s own sanctioned mechanisms. What Defenders Should Do Organizations running Linux infrastructure should take eBPF threats seriously: Audit loaded eBPF programs regularly with bpftool prog list. Know what’s supposed to be there. Restrict eBPF access via kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1 and limit CAP_BPF / CAP_NET_ADMIN. Monitor for magic packets — several eBPF backdoors activate via specific TCP flags or window sizes. Patch aggressively — BPF verifier bugs are a recurring vulnerability class, and weaponized exploits appear fast. Watch for unexpected XDP programs on network interfaces. Gather fresh threat intelligence – stay up to date on new attack vectors, tools and techniques which may help you tailor new detections and enforcement to block eBPF- based malware. The Bottom Line eBPF rootkits represent a genuine evolution in Linux threats as their implants can evade checks focused on loaded kernel modules. LinkPro went further by trying to hide its eBPF programs from bpftool prog list. Investigators could still see associated BPF maps and links, illustrating why defenders should compare multiple sources of host telemetry. Flare found underground posts sharing source code and instructions for hiding processes and activating an implant with a crafted packet. Synacktiv documented both techniques in its investigation of LinkPro, giving defenders a concrete example of how they can appear in an intrusion. Learn more by signing up for our free trial. jb0rdv.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 11, 2026Cyber Attack / Ransomware Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026. Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes. The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments. The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows - CVE-2023-41265 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An HTTP tunneling vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation and allow an attacker to execute HTTP requests on the backend server hosting the repository application. CVE-2023-41266 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate an anonymous session and perform HTTP requests to unauthorized endpoints. CVE-2023-48365 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability that stems from improper validation of HTTP headers, allowing an attacker to elevate their privilege by tunneling HTTP requests and execute HTTP requests on the backend server. It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265. In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink. The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23" on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known. "The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said. Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence. This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files. A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals. "If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator." Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711, indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

fuhcoz.text: Poland temporarily shut down a government platform used by citizens and businesses to access public services after detecting and stopping a cyberattack, officials said Tuesday. The attack targeted ePUAP, a nationwide system that allows users to submit official documents, communicate with government agencies and complete administrative procedures online. Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said security teams responded immediately to the incident and were working to restore the platform's full functionality. "The cyberattack on the state ePUAP system was detected and stopped," Gawkowski said in a social media post. The minister said the infrastructure of Poland's Central Information Technology Center, the government agency responsible for maintaining key digital services, including ePUAP, remained secure. Officials said the ePUAP platform was taken offline as a precaution rather than because of damage caused by the attack. "It's not that the system was somehow compromised or its operation was disrupted by this attack," Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told Polish news agency PAP. "We simply disabled it as a precautionary measure." Authorities have not disclosed how the attack was carried out or who was responsible. There has been no public confirmation that hackers gained access to government systems or stole sensitive information. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring the platform, saying services will resume once security specialists complete their work. According to a notice on the government's website, ePUAP electronic mailboxes remain unavailable to citizens and public institutions. The disruption could also temporarily affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which allows people to access public services and electronically sign official documents. Poland has faced repeated cyberattacks targeting government institutions, critical infrastructure and private companies in recent months. In October, Polish online invoicing provider Fakturownia reported a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners. In September, hackers also stole data from Qbusoft, a Polish healthcare software provider, following a separate breach involving medical technology company MyDr. Polish authorities said the MyDr incident potentially affected information relating to about 19 million people and roughly 12,000 healthcare organizations. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. 1x0xuk3.text: Fourteen governments participating in the Pall Mall Process, a diplomatic effort led by Britain and France to rein in the global spyware industry, adopted their first guidelines for commercial hacking businesses on Wednesday. The French Foreign Ministry said the guidelines, aimed at addressing abuses associated with the proliferation of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities (CCICs), set out “the first global standard of responsible conduct.” “Access to certain capabilities once reserved for a handful of specialized government agencies has gradually widened: any actor can now buy ‘off the shelf’ the ability to silently penetrate a phone,” the ministry said. While it acknowledged those tools have been used in intelligence operations and to tackle organized crime, the ministry warned they “have also been implicated in surveillance campaigns targeting journalists, political officials, activists or businesses.” The guidelines are non-binding and endorsed by governments rather than industry organizations. They call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses. Companies should halt sales and support when serious misuse is a credible risk, according to the text, and are asked to “consider” remedies for victims of human rights abuses. There are no penalties for non-compliance and enforcement pressure is expected to come from governments which buy the tools and license their export. The point of the industry guidelines is “to disincentivise irresponsible activity across the market for CCICs; improve transparency for regulators, vendors and customers; and provide clarity for businesses operating both within and peripherally to the industry,” said the British Foreign Office. The guidelines were endorsed at the Pall Mall initiative’s third conference, attended by representatives from 43 countries. Fewer than half signed up to endorse them, with signatories including the United Kingdom and France, alongside the United States, Germany, Italy and Japan. The guidelines “are voluntary in nature,” the ministry said. “They do not create new international legal obligations and do not call into question uses that states consider legitimate in the fields of national security, defense, the fight against organized crime or cybersecurity. “A voluntary code is not, however, an optional code: one’s word, given before one’s peers, one’s industries and one’s citizens, is a commitment.” The Pall Mall Process has faced persistent challenges since its launch in London in 2024. While that event drew large technology and cybersecurity firms, it did not feature the controversial businesses whose products had been linked to abuses. A year later, participants raised concerns that the initiative lacks the ability to actually change how these tools are traded and used. Some noted that Britain and France were seeking to restrict other states’ access to these tools while championing their own spyware industries. Last year’s conference produced the first code of practice for governments, but no agreement on how to influence company behavior. Twenty-seven countries have since signed the code. It is not clear why the remaining 15 did not endorse the new code on Wednesday. The ministry said participants would continue their work as “artificial intelligence, the growing automation of certain functions and the emergence of new business models” raise new questions for governments and companies. ot7ij1.text: N-able released hotfixes to address zero-day bugs affecting its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, which were publicly disclosed over the weekend and forced it to take vulnerable hosted environments offline. This follows N-able's decision to take all hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions until it could patch them against potential attacks targeting the zero-day flaws in the wild. "N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer on Monday. "As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice." N-central lets IT departments and managed service providers (MSPs) monitor, manage, and maintain client networks and devices from a centralized web-based console. N-able has now released N-central 2026.4 HF2 with security patches and technology updates for some of the leaked zero-days, including "the most critical" vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-125883 - Multiple XXE Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125878 - Multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125879 - Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config CVE-2026-125880 - Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context) CVE-2026-125881 - Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation CVE-2026-125882 - RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security) CVE-2026-91000 - Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation In a Tuesday update, N-able said that all hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all regions have now been successfully upgraded and advised and "strongly" recommended that all N-central On-Premises customers upgrade their installations to the newly released version "as soon as possible." "Customers should follow the published upgrade guidance carefully before restoring normal access to their N-central environment. Earlier incident guidance advised On-Premises customers to keep their N-central servers offline while remediation was being developed," it said. While N-able has yet to flag these flaws as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that attackers have already started scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems and warned admins to take N-central servers offline immediately. "During the past 24 hours, we have observed probing of N-able N-central for the 0-days that were dropped publicly yesterday," Defused said. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth. These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface." Internet security nonprofit Shadowserver reports that just over 148 N-central servers are currently exposed online, a sharp decrease from the 1,338 it detected on Monday. Internet-exposed N-central servers (Shadowserver) Disclosed after previous reports were allegedly ignored Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws. Bales said the zero-day bugs affect N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes that most (if not all) of the flaws also affect earlier versions. The disclosed vulnerabilities include remote code execution (RCE), authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, XML external entity (XXE) injection, and cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws. The security researcher also demoed a critical unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit chain that abuses N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset the targeted account's password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user. Attackers could also use this exploit to create a Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, which provides them rogue admin access to the N-central management interface, as shown in the video demo embedded below. Bales told BleepingComputer that he released the N-central zero-days without notifying N-able because the company allegedly failed to patch vulnerabilities (including two unrelated remote code execution bugs and a privilege-escalation flaw) he reported in a different N-able product about five to six months ago. When asked about Bales' allegations regarding the previously disclosed security issues, N-able did not address the questions and instead responded with a statement about the N-central security incident and precautionary shutdown. 1ul0m0p.text: Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday. They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data. The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said. Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies. According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical. The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text. Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14. Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement. No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected. The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern. Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list. ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say. The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in. To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link". The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it. The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed. An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another. The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes. The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday. By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research. As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default. Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say. With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain. The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report. On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses. How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks: Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account. If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window. Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page. Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed. Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner. In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

1fhg3ub.text: We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. That was true for us at Token as well. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default. This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales. Standards are coming, but there are steps security teams can take today. The agent we would have flagged The agent we created is named Rehearsal. Its job is to answer questions inside the Token platform by doing rather than telling. It autonomously opens pages in the browser tab, sets filters, and fills in forms. From a security perspective, it’s a typical UI agent that runs in the user’s browser. That’s what makes it useful. But it also means the agent runs within the user’s session and has their reach. Moreover, to the server behind the page, the agent’s clicks are inherently indistinguishable from the user’s, because nothing in a session cookie points to who the session driver is. What controlling both sides made possible Because Token owns both the agent and the app it runs, we can close each gap from the inside. For example, Token knows who’s driving the session because Rehearsal tells it who is. We learned that there are multiple best practices that you can apply when you control the AI agent itself: While the agent moves, dim and lock the application and clearly indicate who has control. Record every move for each session, including those that were blocked. Reduce the agent’s reach below the user’s. For Rehearsal, we ensure the dashboards are read-only. It can’t save anything without the user’s approval, doesn’t fill in secret fields, and never sends a call that the platform has refused. It also understands the dashboard controls through the page’s accessibility labels. This works for our own agent, but only because it relies on access that no outside agent has. Who has to fix it for everyone else? We could give Rehearsal an actor, a scope, and a page map because we're the ones who wrote it. A browser agent driving your CRM or your cloud console has none of that. The app can't tell that it’s there, and the agent can't tell which field holds a secret or which button deletes a record. The session itself carries the user's identity. The way out is to give agents their own lanes, separate from human users'. The web has started building them, but it isn't necessarily focused on holistic approaches. The browser can mark when its agent is driving and restrict itself accordingly. Chrome auto-browse, for example, already requires a person’s approval before high-stakes actions such as payments or mass emails, limits its agent to the sites the task requires, and tags the pages the agent visits in the user’s history. Microsoft lets admins turn agentic browsing on per site and pause it before passwords and card numbers are entered. The app can publish its actions as tools. WebMCP, a draft that Google and Microsoft are writing in a W3C community group, lets a site expose actions that an agent can call directly and flag each one as read-only or consequential. That way, the agent doesn't need to guess what a button does. The agent can sign its requests. Web Bot Auth, now an IETF working group draft, lets a site verify which agent sent a request. What’s missing is a layer that connects them. Each lane knows something the others don’t, and none of them passes it on. The browser knows its agent is driving, but neither Chrome nor Edge describes how to tell the app on the other end. A WebMCP tool runs inside the user’s session, with the user’s rights, so it doesn’t, by itself, narrow what the agent can reach. Web Bot Auth names the agent, but the draft makes it plain that it doesn’t cover delegation, so it omits the person the agent works for. The app ends up holding on to pieces of context rather than delivering something actionable. Now consider that the agents are arriving faster than the standards. Agent-friendly isn’t enough on its own. Every lane built for agents should carry the agent’s identity, a verifiable link to the person it acts for, and a scope narrower than that person’s. Together, those three signals give an application the minimum context it needs to make an authorization decision. Otherwise, a faster lane is just a faster path to the misuse of privilege. What security teams can do before standards catch up Waiting for standardization is not an option. You need to start discovering agentic browsers and extensions as soon as possible, including the users whose sessions they borrow. And while you can’t tell who clicked, you can choose which clicks need a person by adding a step-up check such as a passkey prompt. Inventory browser agents, agentic extensions, and endpoint agents that can act through authenticated sessions and map them to users and owners. Trace every AI agent consumer, so you know which people (and other agents) are using each individual agent Review every identity that each individual agent has access to Identify potential attack paths that use agents to bypass access controls Require explicit approval or step-up authentication before sensitive or irreversible application actions. Ask critical SaaS vendors whether their audit records distinguish agent activity from human activity and whether they support task-scoped delegation. Until browsers and applications can carry agent identity, human delegation, and task scope together, companies should treat every agent using a human session as delegated access that must be discovered, constrained, and audited.

cfccdm.text: The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys. Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week. The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week. The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19. Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains. Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise. The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again. The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception. After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says. The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification. The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237. Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed. The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls. Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones. According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took. The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer. As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled. The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18. Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise. Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C. Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says. The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place. Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all. KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30. The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla. Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known. What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement. Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers. All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider. Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines. According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30. macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.

eva7x7.text: Microsoft says the November 2026 cumulative updates resolve USB audio issues plaguing Windows users who have installed security updates released since September. The company explained, when it acknowledged this known issue days after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday, that USB Audio Class 1.0 devices failed to start or produce audio on some systems after installing recent updates. Some affected users reported seeing no audio output, unresponsive volume controls and sound settings, and "This device cannot start (Code 10)." errors in Device Manager, while others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes. These audio issues affect both server (Windows Server 2012 and later) and client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) systems. Microsoft released out-of-band updates on September 14 to fix the symptoms experienced on devices using 8-channel or 3D audio modes and has now addressed the remaining issues in security updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday. "The symptoms are resolved in the Windows security update released on November 10, 2026 (KB5132061) and later updates," Microsoft said in a Windows release health dashboard update. "We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one." While Microsoft has yet to provide an official workaround for those who can't immediately install the November 2026 security updates, some users have restored audio on affected Windows PCs by switching to 2-channel mode. Previous audio issues affecting Windows systems Two years ago, Microsoft also confirmed an issue that caused game audio to unexpectedly increase to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers due to blue screen of death (BSOD) issues. In January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue triggered by the KB5050094 optional preview cumulative update, which caused audio playback issues and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers. More recently, in September 2025, it lifted a safeguard hold preventing Windows 11 24H2 upgrades on systems with Dirac audio improvement software because compatibility issues caused Bluetooth speakers and headsets to malfunction. With the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft also resolved Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems triggered by the October 2026 Windows Server security updates. 1r7gly.text: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned on Tuesday that hackers are now exploiting a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability in attacks. Cisco BroadWorks is a cloud unified communications (UC) software platform and the underlying engine allowing telecom carriers and managed service providers (MSPs) to provide branded cloud PBX, voice, and collaboration services to business customers. Tracked as CVE-2026-20320, the security flaw stems from an improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) reference weakness in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML Parser that can allow unauthenticated, remote attackers to read sensitive configuration information from vulnerable systems by sending maliciously crafted XML messages. "This vulnerability exists because XML entries are improperly parsed due to external entity resolution being allowed by default. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted XML message to the Open Client Interface - Provisioning (OCI-P) service," Cisco explained when it patched the bug in August. CISA flagged CVE-2026-20320 as actively exploited and added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems within two weeks, by November 24, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, CISA urged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patches for this vulnerability to defend their networks against ongoing attacks. "These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," it warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities." Targeted in autonomous AI attack While CISA didn't share more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-20320 in the wild, threat intelligence firm Malbear Labs said over the weekend that a Chinese-speaking threat actor has exploited the flaw with the help of a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash artificial intelligence model in attacks targeting a European telecommunications provider and thirteen organizations that used its data centers and cloud infrastructure. The attack focused on the telecom provider's BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), and Malbear Labs found that the BroadWorks Provisioning Server (which stores subscriber configuration for all users) was also exposed via an unauthenticated directory listing. "The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser. A crafted OCI request to port 2208 causes the XML parser to read arbitrary files from the server filesystem and no prior authentication required," Malbear Labs said. "From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication." Since November 2021, CISA has added 103 Cisco vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, seven of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs. 1y6i3pn.text: Microsoft has fixed Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems after installing the October 2026 Windows Server security updates. Microsoft acknowledged this known issue in mid-October, confirming that users had trouble accessing email or signing in to Outlook after installing the latest updates on systems running Windows Server 2019 and later. As explained at the time, the sign-in and mail flow issues are caused by a new default limit on the amount of memory Endpoint Mapper uses when handling Endpoint Lookup calls, introduced by the October 2026 updates. "After installing the October 2026 Windows security update [..], some on-premises Exchange servers might experience issues accessing or sending email. Users might be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web (OWA), or email messages sent from Outlook might remain in the Outbox and not be delivered. Additionally, Exchange might experience issues accessing mailboxes during mailbox replication," Microsoft said at the time. "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem," it added in a separate blog describing the issues. However, Microsoft said that this Outlook on the web (OWA) known issue isn't linked to the October 2026 Exchange server security updates and urged customers not to uninstall them. Fixed by November Patch Tuesday updates In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates (KB5131080 and KB5131090) address this known issue and advised affected users to install them on all affected systems. Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround that should resolve these issues for those who can't immediately deploy this month's cumulative updates, which requires modifying a registry key on affected Exchange Server systems. To do that, IT administrators have to run the following command from an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange Server to increase the maximum number of Endpoint Lookup calls and the amount of memory that Endpoint Mapper can use, and then restart the device: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f After the system reboots, the admins should monitor the Exchange environment and raise the Endpoint Mapper memory limit if it recurs.
