They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no, including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no. The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys. "If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says. Why Long Passwords Work Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt(), the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field. An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash. For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored *, so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password. This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks. The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then. The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem. Why the Fix Came the Next Day Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement, he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours. No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

e6o6qp.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT. Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections. "The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage. The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure. However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode. "The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained. "By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode." Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat. What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link. That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026. "Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said. "The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them." The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation. "The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts." "The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response." The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions - An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them. A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation. A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request." A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior. A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text. A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload. A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions. A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI." An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing. A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse." A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections. A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions. A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration." A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access." A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues. "Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. an6e8t.text: The Baker Tilly Advisory Group is notifying clients that a data breach has compromised certain personal information about them and their dependents. The company said the exposed data was stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider Baker Tilly uses to serve clients. Baker Tilly learned of the incident on September 6 and completed its review of the affected data on October 28, when it identified whose information was involved. “On September 6, 2026, Baker Tilly became aware of a potential cybersecurity incident involving certain information stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider used by Baker Tilly in connection with services we provide to clients,” reads the notification to customers. “The unauthorized actor was able to obtain data relating to certain Baker Tilly clients,” the company added. The breach notification does not provide a count of impacted clients, does not name the service provider, and leaves the specific data types exposed as a placeholder. Data from the Office of the Texas Attorney General reports that Baker Tilly impacted 10,456 individuals in the state of Texas alone. The portal lists Social Security numbers (SSNs), full names, addresses, and other information as exposed data types. Baker Tilly is a major accounting firm in the U.S., providing auditing, tax planning, compliance, advisory, and business operations services. Globally, the company operates in 147 countries and reports an annual revenue of $6.8 billion. After discovering the incident, the company says it took immediate steps to contain it, contracted external experts to investigate, and notified law enforcement authorities. Furthermore, it says it currently has no evidence of unauthorized activity on its own network, and added that it has no reports of identity theft or fraud linked to the exposure of customer information. To mitigate the risks arising from the incident, the firm offers affected individuals 24 months of credit and identity monitoring through Experian. BleepingComputer has contacted Baker Tilly for more information about the data breach, its source, the number of affected customers, and the type of data compromised, but we have not received a reply by the time of publishing. 1b4qibx.text: Certificate authority eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate CA certificates after an investigation into its recent certificate security incident found improper handling of private keys during the certificate-generation process. The new revocations bring the total number of affected intermediate CA certificates to 16, including eight previously compromised certificates whose private keys were so weak that anyone could recover them almost instantly. In a new incident report published Tuesday, eMudhra said that both sets of certificates were affected by a custom Python script used to transfer private keys between hardware security modules (HSMs) in April 2025. HSMs are devices designed to securely generate and store cryptographic keys, preventing sensitive private keys from being exposed outside the hardware. eMudhra says it developed the script to move certificate authority keys between different HSM vendors at its facilities after delays in obtaining new hardware. However, the script contained a bug that reduced eight ECDSA private keys to a single byte, making them extremely easy to recover. The same script also processed eight RSA private keys, which handled sensitive key information in the memory of the computer running the script rather than keeping it protected within the HSM. While the RSA keys were not weakened like the original eight certificates, eMudhra says it could not demonstrate that it handled them under its certificate security policies. "A re‑import performed from host process memory is not consistent with the CPS §6.2.6 and the RSA objects are therefore treated as not meeting that requirement," reads the incident report. Due to this, the company revoked the additional eight RSA intermediate CA certificates on November 7, including certificates used to issue TLS and code-signing certificates. Some of the affected RSA intermediates had been actively issuing certificates since May 2026, with the last certificate issued on November 3. eMudhra says the affected customer certificates have also been replaced or migrated. The investigation also found that an earlier problem in June 2025 could have revealed the flaw more than a year before it was discovered by a security researcher known as "Wayne." At that time, eMudhra detected certificate revocation lists (CRLs) signed with private keys that did not match the corresponding CA certificates. The company fixed the issue by signing the revocation lists with the matching keys but did not investigate why the problem occurred. The new report confirms this was an early warning sign of the faulty key-generation process that went undetected until October 2026. The investigation also found that eMudhra did not verify the strength of generated private keys or check that the keys used for certification matched those originally created in the HSM. Major browsers blocked compromised certificates As BleepingComputer previously reported, the incident was first disclosed on October 17, when a security researcher named Wayne discovered that eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys could be recovered by testing just 256 possible values. Major browsers and operating systems trusted the compromised certificates, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications. Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors subsequently released protections to block the compromised certificates. Microsoft also released out-of-band Windows updates on October 26 to remove trust in affected eMudhra certificate trust chains on systems that could not receive automatic certificate trust updates. Following the incident, eMudhra announced that it would exit the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and transition its remaining customers to another provider. The company says it plans to stop issuing certificates under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16. eMudhra has also commissioned an independent review by KPMG, with findings expected by December 4, to identify improvements to its certificate management and key-generation procedures. The company says it has not detected any evidence that the compromised keys were used maliciously. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 16iakw7.text: Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces. The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers. Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts. Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data. Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3. However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users. Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text. Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI. The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled. “Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update. "Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.” Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data. According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts. Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats. If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset. 1pryxd1.text: ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices. The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise. "Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit. "We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us." ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices. According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment. The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device. It is unclear how this reported reverse-pivot technique works, including whether it exploits a software vulnerability or abuses legitimate ScreenConnect functionality. In a statement to BleepingComputer, ConnectWise confirmed it is investigating the attacks and urged partners to avoid interactive remote sessions with potentially compromised devices. "We are aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and are actively investigating," ConnectWise told BleepingComputer. "As a precaution, partners should avoid opening interactive ScreenConnect sessions to suspected compromised devices and use separate security tooling to investigate. Partners should also review account activity, revoke active sessions, reset credentials from a trusted device, and verify multifactor authentication." The company said it would provide further information and guidance through the ConnectWise Trust Center. Huntress has not yet determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says their current telemetry points to compromised credentials and hijacked MSP support sessions. Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised. “Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts,” Huntress told BleepingComputer. Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers. The indicators include: Attacker relay: 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen) C2 domains: newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org Possible additional C2: cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com Secondary C2: sc.payproofkit[.]com (155.94.150[.]39, hostname: WIN-FB5CKHMU4E1) Stager: hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4 Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091 Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N> Attacker name: Addmin Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, Run-Lateral-Full.bat The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints. BleepingComputer reached out to Huntress with additional questions about the attacks and will update the post if we receive a response. Earlier malware activity linked to rogue ScreenConnect identifier BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed. The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat [VirusTotal], appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026. The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key. It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers. VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com, with digitaldownloads[.]com listed by Huntress as a potential IOC. DigitalDownloads ScreenConnect portal Source: BleepingComputer After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091, one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress. If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram. The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it may have been used in phishing attacks. 7ocoy1.text: The U.S. accused three men of orchestrating attacks across Europe on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), including a London arson incident that was recorded for propaganda. An indictment unsealed Tuesday says the broader campaign, targeting Jewish and American sites, included attacks on synagogues in Belgium, the Netherlands and London, and U.S. bank buildings in Amsterdam and Paris. It also included a stabbing in London that left two Jewish men seriously injured. Prosecutors say the same network later plotted to attack RAF Fairford, a British air base used by U.S. bombers, with vans and what the plotters intended to be explosives. During the attack one suspect directed the vans toward the base by phone from Iran, while another, already jailed in New York, relayed coded instructions through calls with relatives. The superseding indictment adds two defendants to a case against Mohammad al-Saadi, an alleged commander of the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah who has been jailed in New York since May. The additional defendants are Mohsen Mohajeri, whom prosecutors identify as an IRGC operative, and Mohammed Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi who once lived in Britain. Both are at large and believed to be in Iran. All three face terrorism charges carrying potential life sentences. Prosecutors say that recording the attempted attacks for propaganda was an essential part of the network’s operations. The indictment includes images of them directing attacks from a room in Iraq, as well as recordings of instructions given to the attackers. During an arson attack on a Jewish charity's building in London in April, al-Hassani told the attacker to “light one in your hand,” “light it” and “throw the fourth one,” according to the indictment. The attack was streamed over FaceTime and projected onto a large screen with the militia’s logo. The IRGC operative filmed the proceedings and the men directing it. Two days earlier, al-Hassani allegedly directed another arson attack on Iran International, a London-based media organization that has repeatedly faced attacks from the Iranian regime. Again over a video call, al-Hassani told the attacker to get close to the gate and ensure he could see what was happening on camera. During another attack on a London synagogue the following day, he urged the attacker to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” In March, when al-Saadi asked the IRGC operative Mohajeri about working with his militia on joint attacks involving drones and missiles, Mohajeri agreed and told him to “make sure to photograph a video and pictures.” The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or HAYI, which prosecutors describe as a front for Kataib Hezbollah and the IRGC. The group claimed about 18 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe between March and April, beginning days after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran. HAYI also claimed that drones carrying radioactive material had targeted the Israeli Embassy in London, although police found no hazardous material after investigating the incident. Al-Saadi had received videos days earlier showing men in hazmat suits posing beside a drone that had been fitted with vials of an unspecified white powder. Hybrid Theory The new indictment gives the most detailed account yet of how the attacks were directed from afar — drawing on recordings, images and messages exchanged across several apps — and comes amid concerns over what Western authorities describe as “hybrid warfare” and “state-sponsored terrorism.” Much of the evidence comes from al-Saadi's own iPhone, which FBI agents seized after he was first detained in Turkey in May. Prosecutors say it contained recordings of FaceTime calls, raw attack footage and messages with a Kataib Hezbollah contact. FaceTime calls are end-to-end encrypted, meaning Apple cannot access their content while the calls are ongoing, however investigators were able to obtain recordings stored on al-Saadi’s seized phone. The seizure of this evidence comes amid disputes over law enforcement access to encrypted data, particularly in Europe and the United Kingdom. Apple is currently challenging a reported British demand for access to protected iCloud data, while the European Commission has outlined plans to explore technical options for lawful access to encrypted evidence. Images in the new indictment show what prosecutors say are Mohajeri and al-Hassani planning attacks while sitting in front of a laptop displaying a map of London, as well as stills from videos of the men directing attacks live. Earlier images of al-Saadi show him mingling with senior Iranian and militia commanders. These came from his phone and social media accounts, prosecutors said. The FBI linked his WhatsApp, Snapchat, Telegram and X accounts through a single phone number. Earlier filings say al-Saadi received raw footage of a bombing of a synagogue in Liège, Belgium, through Telegram and used the app to send footage of an arson attack on Jewish volunteer ambulances in London to a contact saved in his phone as a China-based media company. Prosecutors also say al-Saadi paid an undercover officer about $3,000 in cryptocurrency in April, which was related to a planned attack on a Manhattan synagogue. The nature of the transaction was not detailed, and no attack took place. In August, al-Hassani allegedly paid someone to film the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase, which houses U.S. military aircraft and personnel. The following month, paid associates bought vans, barrels of fuel and metal objects that could serve as shrapnel, and researched buying chemicals, according to the indictment. During the alleged attempted attack towards the end of that month, al-Hassani was described as being in frequent contact by phone with the drivers of three vans heading toward the base, directing their movements from Iran, prosecutors say. It is not clear whether he used normal voice calls or communicated via an app. At least two of the vans were turned back at a security roadblock. British authorities recovered the vehicles in the early hours of the next morning and arrested their occupants. Police said at the time they found no explosives but seized petrol. Seven people were arrested and released on bail. Apple, Snap, X and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Al-Saadi's X account, which the FBI says had posted calls for revenge against Americans as early as 2020, remained online Wednesday. 1kkzi6q.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 11, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on affected systems. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access. CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS score: 8.1) - An origin validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access. Successful exploitation of either of the shortcomings could permit remote attackers to escalate privileges without requiring any special permissions or access. While CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.1.5, CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions starting from 7.1.0 and before 7.1.8. Earlier this July, the popular videoconferencing platform shipped fixes for another improper input validation flaw impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows (CVE-2026-53412, CVSS score: 9.8) that could enable an unauthenticated user to take control of accounts. Although Zoom makes no mention of the vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, users are advised to apply the latest patches to mitigate potential threats.
